claim_evidence.claim: The article’s original-publication line identifies ‘Williams and Nagel, “Moral Luck”’ as a 1976 Proceedings of the Aristotelian Society Supplementary Volume publication; the dataset repeats that attribution.
claim_evidence.finding: The bibliographic records distinguish Williams’s ‘Moral Luck’ (1976, Proceedings of the Aristotelian Society, Supplementary Volume L, 115–135) from Nagel’s ‘Moral Luck’ (1979, Mortal Questions). Williams’s own 1981 acknowledgements identify the former; the SEP bibliography separately lists Williams (1976) and Nagel (1979), and the Nagel reproduction identifies Mortal Questions (1979). The article’s line and dataset therefore misleadingly bundle the two as a joint 1976 publication.
claim_evidence.limitation: The Nagel copy is a university-hosted reproduction rather than a publisher-hosted original; its page labels conflict, but the source note and SEP bibliography agree on 1979 Mortal Questions. The 1976 Williams pagination is also given in Williams’s own acknowledgements.
claim_evidence.location: Williams, Moral Luck: Philosophical Papers 1973–1980, acknowledgements p. xiii; SEP bibliography entries ‘Nagel, Thomas, 1979’ and ‘Williams, Bernard, 1976’; Nagel reproduction essay header p. 24
claim_evidence.source_title: Williams, ‘Moral Luck’ (1981 reprint); Nagel, ‘Moral Luck’ (1979); SEP, ‘Moral Luck’

claim_evidence.claim: The scenario has a lorry driver obeying every rule, a child runs into the road and is killed, and nothing reasonably available to the driver could have prevented it.
claim_evidence.finding: Williams’s text describes a lorry driver who ‘through no fault of his’ runs over a child and emphasizes his distinctive relation to the event. The SEP describes a pair of fully precautionary, rule-abiding drivers in a related example involving a dog, and explains the no-fault child case as a case where the driver could have done nothing else. Nagel also treats the entirely faultless driver separately from negligent cases. Thus the no-fault core is supported, but the article’s exact ‘every rule’/‘carefully’ wording combines source formulations and should be stated as the article’s stipulation rather than a verbatim detail of Williams’s case.
claim_evidence.limitation: Williams’s 1981 chapter is a revised reprint; the article’s careful-driving stipulation is a reasonable composite, but should not be presented as a verbatim feature of the original Williams example.
claim_evidence.location: Williams chapter 2, p. 29; SEP §1, paragraph on the two fully precautionary drivers and paragraph on Williams’s no-fault driver; Nagel reproduction, running p. 204
claim_evidence.source_title: Williams, ‘Moral Luck’ (1981 reprint); SEP, ‘Moral Luck’; Nagel, ‘Moral Luck’

claim_evidence.claim: The second driver provides a comparison between an equally careful (or equally careless) journey that ends without incident.
claim_evidence.finding: The SEP’s §1 discussion presents a no-fault comparison between two careful drivers and separately discusses negligence variants in which consequences differ. Nagel’s text distinguishes an entirely faultless driver from a driver with even slight negligence and describes how the outcome changes the latter’s self-blame. This supports the teaching comparison as a composite, not a single Williams scenario.
claim_evidence.limitation: The article’s own line 59 says added comparisons are teaching prompts, not established historical variations; preserve that limitation and distinguish the careful and negligent cases.
claim_evidence.location: SEP §1, paragraphs on fully precautionary drivers and the negligent-driver/brake-failure variant; Nagel reproduction, running pp. 204–205

claim_evidence.claim: Williams uses the no-fault driver to illustrate a first-person regret distinct from bystander sympathy, which remains even when he is not at fault.
claim_evidence.finding: Williams explicitly contrasts the driver’s feeling with a spectator’s and says the driver has a special relation to the event that is not eliminated by the fact that it was not his fault. The SEP calls this ‘agent-regret’ and describes distinctive first-person thought and possible reparative expression. The article’s core attribution and distinction are supported.
claim_evidence.limitation: Agent-regret is not by itself a finding of guilt or blame. The SEP and Nagel distinguish it from moral assessment and from cases of negligence.
claim_evidence.location: Williams chapter 2, p. 29; SEP §3.1, paragraphs beginning ‘Williams elucidates a notion of “agent-regret”’ and quoting Williams on the lorry driver

claim_evidence.claim: The central problem is a tension between a control-based principle of moral assessment and actual assessment practices affected by outcomes beyond control.
claim_evidence.finding: The SEP states and explains the Control Principle and its corollary, then develops the conflict with ordinary judgments; Nagel says the extension of the control condition threatens to erode familiar moral assessments. The article’s framing is accurate as a summary, not a proof that one side is correct.
claim_evidence.limitation: Neither source settles the philosophical dispute. The article appropriately states a question rather than claiming a definitive solution.
claim_evidence.location: SEP Introduction and §1, paragraphs defining the Control Principle and outlining the problem; Nagel reproduction, running pp. 203–204

claim_evidence.claim: The article says many ethical traditions hold responsibility should not depend on luck, and that ordinary practice treats careless drivers who cause deaths differently from those who do not.
claim_evidence.finding: The SEP ties the control principle to Kantian inspiration and gives cases of differential assessment of negligent outcomes. Nagel discusses differential legal and moral treatment for negligent harm and no-harm outcomes. These sources support the narrower control-principle and practice claims, but not the broad unsourced generalization to ‘many ethical traditions.’
claim_evidence.limitation: The broad claim about multiple ethical traditions is not established by this one SEP entry or the consulted primary passages; ‘a prominent control-based principle’ is more proportionate.
claim_evidence.location: SEP §1, opening paragraphs on Kant and the Control Principle; SEP §1 types of resultant luck; Nagel reproduction, running pp. 204–205

claim_evidence.claim: The article says the case bears on law, medicine, and engineering, where outcomes often determine accountability.
claim_evidence.finding: The SEP has a dedicated §2.1 on legal responsibility and punishment and discusses outcome-sensitive criminal and tort law. The consulted passages do not establish the article’s parallel generalization about medicine and engineering, nor the unqualified phrase ‘often determine accountability’ across these fields.
claim_evidence.limitation: No medicine- or engineering-specific source was consulted, so those applications remain unsupported. The article may present them as illustrative questions or add suitable sources.
claim_evidence.location: SEP §2.1, ‘Legal Responsibility and Punishment,’ especially paragraphs on attempts/completed crimes and negligence/tort law

claim_evidence.claim: The article’s major-interpretations section distinguishes control-based views, Williams-associated agent-regret views, and a skeptical position associated with Nagel.
claim_evidence.finding: The SEP discusses control-based explanations, the distinction between agent-regret and moral blame, Nagel’s skeptical argument, acceptance and rejection of moral luck, and a variety of mixed approaches. Nagel’s essay itself describes the control problem as a paradox and presses its skeptical force. The article’s labels are a fair introductory sketch but do not represent mutually exclusive or exhaustive camps.
claim_evidence.limitation: Latus challenges an inference Williams draws from agent-regret to retrospective rational justification; the article does not make that inference. Do not imply that the three labels exhaust the debate or that Nagel’s skeptical pressure is the only scholarly response.
claim_evidence.location: SEP §§3–4, particularly §3.1 on agent-regret and §4 on acceptance of moral luck; Nagel reproduction, running pp. 203–204; Latus §1 and §2 opening
claim_evidence.source_title: SEP, ‘Moral Luck’; Nagel, ‘Moral Luck’; Latus, ‘Moral Luck’

claim_evidence.claim: The article says Nagel distinguishes several kinds of luck, including circumstantial, constitutive, and outcome luck; negligent variants show how fault and consequence interact.
claim_evidence.finding: Nagel lists roughly four kinds: constitutive, circumstantial, causal antecedents, and the way actions/projects turn out. He explicitly says the fully faultless driver’s agent-regret is not yet moral bad luck, then contrasts it with a driver whose slight negligence contributes to a child’s death. The article’s use of ‘including’ is accurate, but the no-fault/regret versus negligence/resultant-luck distinction should be made explicit in its explanation.
claim_evidence.limitation: The article does not claim its list is exhaustive; this finding recommends clarifying the key distinction, not adding detail for its own sake.
claim_evidence.location: Nagel reproduction, running pp. 204–205; SEP §1, quoted typology of resultant, circumstantial, constitutive, and causal luck

claim_evidence.claim: The article says the example does not make the driver guilty, does not imply outcomes should always be blamed, and that legal liability, blame, and personal regret can diverge.
claim_evidence.finding: Williams’s no-fault passage and Nagel’s explicit distinction between the blameless driver’s agent-regret and negligence-based moral bad luck support the caution against equating regret with guilt. The SEP distinguishes kinds of moral assessment and discusses legal responsibility/punishment separately. The qualification is sound, though the article’s legal-liability distinction is a synthesis rather than a direct quotation from the lorry-driver passage.
claim_evidence.limitation: ‘Legal liability’ has distinct legal meanings not detailed in this article; retain the statement as a caution about distinctions, not a claim that legal and moral standards coincide.
claim_evidence.location: Williams chapter 2, p. 29; Nagel reproduction, running p. 204; SEP §1 discussion of moral-assessment types and §2.1, ‘Legal Responsibility and Punishment’
claim_evidence.source_title: Williams, ‘Moral Luck’ (1981 reprint); Nagel, ‘Moral Luck’; SEP, ‘Moral Luck’

issues.article_claim: Line 6 says ‘Williams and Nagel, “Moral Luck”’ was published in the Proceedings of the Aristotelian Society Supplementary Volume in 1976; the dataset repeats this in original_publication.
issues.evidence_basis: Williams’s acknowledgements (1981 reprint, p. xiii) identify Williams’s 1976 paper and its pages; the SEP bibliography separately lists Williams (1976) and Nagel’s Mortal Questions (1979); the Nagel text reproduction identifies Mortal Questions (1979). The wording conflates separate works and misstates Nagel’s publication date/source.
issues.recommended_action: Separate the attributions: cite Williams’s 1976 Proceedings paper and Nagel’s 1979 ‘Moral Luck’ in Mortal Questions as distinct publications. Correct the dataset field as well as article line 6; do not describe them as a jointly published 1976 item.

issues.article_claim: Lines 13–15 present a careful, rule-abiding driver and the no-fault child death as Williams’s lorry-driver setup; line 23 says ordinary practice treats the careless driver who kills differently from the one who does not.
issues.evidence_basis: Williams’s p. 29 passage establishes the through-no-fault driver and agent-regret, but does not specify meticulous rule compliance. The SEP’s careful-driver comparison is a distinct dog example; Nagel distinguishes the entirely blameless driver from a negligent driver whose negligence contributes to death, and says the former case is not yet moral bad luck.
issues.recommended_action: Mark careful rule-following as an editorial stipulation or use Williams’s wording ‘through no fault’; explicitly separate the no-fault agent-regret case from the negligent resultant-luck variant before drawing conclusions about differential blame.

issues.article_claim: Line 25 generalizes that law, medicine, and engineering often determine accountability by outcomes.
issues.evidence_basis: SEP §2.1 supports a connection to legal responsibility, punishment, criminal law, and tort law. The consulted source does not establish the medicine/engineering generalization or the breadth of ‘often’ across those fields.
issues.recommended_action: Either recast the sentence as an editorial application/question, or add and read suitable discipline-specific sources before retaining the factual generalization.

issues.article_claim: Line 23 generalizes that ‘many ethical traditions’ say moral responsibility should not depend on luck; line 29 presents three ‘Major Interpretations’ as a compact map.
issues.evidence_basis: The SEP frames the central control principle as Kantian-inspired and distinguishes multiple forms of moral assessment, skeptical and anti-skeptical replies, and mixed approaches. It does not establish a broad survey of many traditions or a three-camp exhaustive taxonomy.
issues.recommended_action: Prefer ‘a prominent control-based principle’ and label the three categories a simplified, non-exhaustive teaching map; note that some views combine or qualify approaches.

article_edit_recommendations: Correct the publication metadata in the article and dataset: Williams’s paper is the 1976 Proceedings of the Aristotelian Society Supplementary Volume L article (pp. 115–135); Nagel’s separate essay is in Mortal Questions (1979).

Separate the negligent-driver variant from the no-fault case: identify negligence as a changed premise and explain that Nagel treats the faultless driver’s agent-regret as not yet moral bad luck.
Narrow ‘many ethical traditions’ to a control-based principle and describe the interpretation categories as non-exhaustive and potentially overlapping.
Recast the law/medicine/engineering sentence as an illustrative application, or source each domain-specific claim. Add direct primary references for Williams and Nagel alongside the SEP reference.

Keep the article’s note that the expanded variants are teaching prompts, not historical quotations or settled scholarly versions; distinguish the source’s arguments from the article’s own prompts and inferences.
entries.summary: Relevant passages in the complete SEP reference entry and passages in the primary Williams and Nagel texts were independently accessed and read. The article’s core description of Williams’s no-fault driver and agent-regret is substantially supported, and its broad map of the control problem is recognizable. Two qualifications are material: Nagel distinguishes the blameless driver’s agent-regret from moral bad luck, which is illustrated by a negligent-driver variant; and the article/dataset metadata conflate Williams’s 1976 paper with Nagel’s separate 1979 Moral Luck essay. The SEP supports the legal relevance of outcome-sensitive responsibility, but the article’s medicine and engineering generalization is not established by the cited source. The major-views section is a useful simplification, not an exhaustive or mutually exclusive map. Because material assertions remain unqualified or require correction, recommend partially_source_checked. This is not a claim of expert review or scholarly consensus.

claim_evidence.claim: In Plato’s dialogue, Socrates meets Euthyphro, who is confident that he knows what piety is; Socrates asks whether piety is loved by the gods because it is pious or pious because they love it (article §§1, 5).
claim_evidence.finding: The primary text’s opening presents them at the Porch of the King Archon and has Euthyphro claim exact knowledge. In the 9e–11b passage, Socrates poses the question after Euthyphro defines piety as what all the gods love. The SEP overview identifies the passage at 10a and describes the same context.
claim_evidence.limitation: The text establishes what the Platonic characters say, not that the dialogue’s Socrates is identical in every respect to the historical Socrates. The SEP shorter-works entry explicitly calls the speaker the Platonic figure.
claim_evidence.location: Opening dialogue; Stephanus 9e–11b (Stephanus locator given in the SEP overview; MIT text page itself does not print Stephanus numbers).

claim_evidence.claim: Replacing ‘pious’ with ‘morally good’ and ‘the gods’ with ‘God’ yields the question whether something is good because God commands it or commanded because it is good (article §1).
claim_evidence.finding: This is a modern interpretive reformulation, not the wording of Plato’s dialogue. IEP section 3 explicitly presents a version asking whether God commands an action because it is morally right or it is right because God commands it. SEP describes the Euthyphro question as bearing on theological accounts of morality.
claim_evidence.limitation: The article correctly signals a replacement/generalization, but this is not a direct translation of Plato’s question; the move from piety and Greek gods to goodness, command, and a monotheistic God is an interpretive application.
claim_evidence.location: Section 3, ‘A Persistent Problem: The Euthyphro Dilemma,’ paragraph beginning ‘For our purposes, it will be useful to rephrase Socrates’ question.’

claim_evidence.claim: The dilemma asks whether a moral standard depends on divine will or holds independently of any will, including God’s (article §2).
claim_evidence.finding: The formulation tracks the modern dilemma as discussed in IEP section 3 and the SEP’s account of divine will/command theories and the Euthyphro objection. SEP also records theories that distinguish goodness from rightness or locate the standard in God’s character, so the summary is a useful framing question rather than an exhaustive map of positions.
claim_evidence.limitation: The question compresses several different theories of goodness, rightness, obligation, and divine command; not all are captured by a simple will-versus-independent-standard dichotomy.
claim_evidence.location: Paragraph beginning ‘Socrates (c. 470–399)’ and discussion beginning ‘One recent development in analytic ethical theory.’
claim_evidence.source_title: Religion and Morality in Western Philosophy

claim_evidence.claim: If goodness depends only on command, even cruelty could be good if commanded and divine goodness risks becoming empty; if God commands an act because it is good, goodness has a source independent of God (article §3).
claim_evidence.finding: IEP section 3 explicitly presents the cruelty implication and the concern that a standard independent of God would make God a recognizer rather than author of morality. It also discusses Alston’s response that God’s necessarily good character can be the supreme standard, illustrating that these are argued consequences, not uncontested conclusions. SEP likewise describes the arbitrariness objection and named responses.
claim_evidence.limitation: These are conditional formulations of objections to particular versions of divine-command theory. ‘It seems’ and ‘risks’ appropriately signal argument rather than settled fact; specify that commands alone or a particular account of obligation is at issue.
claim_evidence.location: Section 3, paragraphs beginning ‘A defender of Divine Command Theory might respond’ and ‘Most advocates of Divine Command Theory.’ See also Section 4.c, ‘Alston’s Advice.’

claim_evidence.claim: The argument can bear on whether standards beyond theology can be authoritative and non-arbitrary, including social conventions, laws, and natural-law theories (article §3); the majority-approval analogy is also offered (article §7).
claim_evidence.finding: These are the article’s own pedagogical extensions. The sources consulted discuss moral authority, natural law, and command theories, but do not establish the article’s exact analogies to law, majority opinion, or customs as historical variants of Plato’s argument. The article labels its comparison as a question/variation and its attribution note calls additional comparisons teaching prompts.
claim_evidence.limitation: Treat as analogy and editorial framing, not as an attribution to Plato or a claim that the same argument applies unchanged across domains.
claim_evidence.location: Article §§3 and 7; compare SEP discussion of natural-law theories in ‘The long tradition of philosophical reflection on the virtues and natural law.’
claim_evidence.source_title: Religion and Morality in Western Philosophy

claim_evidence.claim: Divine-command theorists accept the first horn but argue God’s nature is essentially good; natural-law and rationalist views accept the second horn; modified views locate goodness in God’s nature and make the choice a false dichotomy; secular critics use the argument to show moral authority need not be divine (article §4).
claim_evidence.finding: The sources identify multiple named positions, but not these categorical school-wide mappings. SEP distinguishes Quinn, Adams, Hare, and Zagzebski, including Adams’s separation of good and right; it separately describes varieties and disagreements within natural-law approaches. IEP sections 4.a–d discuss distinct replies, including Ockham, human nature, Alston’s supreme-standard account, and modified divine-command theory. The sources show some views addressing one or both horns but do not warrant assigning all theorists in each named tradition to one horn or treating all modified accounts as equivalent. No consulted passage establishes that ‘secular critics’ as a class deploy the dilemma for the stated conclusion.
claim_evidence.limitation: The article’s classifications are broader than the evidence read. This review does not infer a scholarly consensus; it identifies representative named views only.
claim_evidence.location: Discussion beginning ‘One recent development in analytic ethical theory’ and discussion beginning ‘The long tradition of philosophical reflection on the virtues and natural law’; compare IEP sections 3 and 4.a–d.
claim_evidence.source_title: Religion and Morality in Western Philosophy

claim_evidence.claim: The dilemma does not prove God does not exist or show religious ethics is irrational; it identifies a structural problem, and major traditions have long-developed answers (article §5).
claim_evidence.finding: The primary text addresses the definition of piety and does not argue for or against God’s existence. SEP says Socrates’ view at this point is not an objection to connecting morality and religion, and both SEP and IEP discuss particular replies. Those sources support the caution against treating the dilemma as a proof of atheism, while ‘major traditions’ and ‘long-developed answers’ are too broad without naming which traditions or positions.
claim_evidence.limitation: The evidence supports the article’s anti-overstatement qualification, not a comprehensive survey of every religious or philosophical tradition. ‘Major’ is undefined and may imply broader coverage than was checked.
claim_evidence.location: Discussion beginning ‘Socrates (c. 470–399)’; later discussion of divine-command theory and natural law. Compare IEP section 4, ‘Responses to the Euthyphro Dilemma.’
claim_evidence.source_title: Religion and Morality in Western Philosophy

claim_evidence.claim: In Plato’s dialogue the topic is piety and the gods, not one monotheistic deity; later moral-command formulations are uses of Plato’s question (article §5).
claim_evidence.finding: The primary dialogue has Euthyphro and Socrates discuss what is loved by all the gods, while SEP describes the context as Greek religious thought and distinguishes this question from its later use in theological accounts of morality. This accurately marks the original setting versus a later application.
claim_evidence.limitation: ‘The gods of Athenian religion’ is a contextual description, not a phrase supplied by the primary passage. The article’s distinction between the dialogue and the later monotheistic application is important and should remain explicit.
claim_evidence.location: Stephanus 9e–11b, especially Euthyphro’s ‘what all the gods love’; context at the opening; SEP overview paragraph beginning ‘Socrates (c. 470–399).’

claim_evidence.claim: Plato’s Euthyphro is dated to the fourth century BCE (article metadata §§1 and 10; dataset original_publication).
claim_evidence.finding: The MIT page’s hosting metadata says ‘Written 380 B.C.E.’, and SEP classifies Euthyphro among Plato’s shorter ethical dialogues generally considered early in his career. These sources are compatible with the article’s broad fourth-century period, but the primary dialogue cannot establish its own composition date.
claim_evidence.limitation: The SEP passage gives relative chronology, not a precise composition date; the 380 BCE date is host-page metadata, not a statement by Plato or a dating argument in the text. Keep the article’s broad approximation and avoid suggesting greater precision.
claim_evidence.location: Opening paragraph on the shorter ethical works’ early placement; Section 13, ‘Euthyphro.’ Compare MIT page header metadata, ‘Written 380 B.C.E.’

claim_evidence.claim: The article’s source note says SEP Religion and Morality was consulted and Plato’s dialogue was not independently retrieved; dataset reference points to the same SEP entry (article §10 and dataset record).
claim_evidence.finding: The statement matches the dataset’s one reference, URL, kind, and stated support. The article’s added explanatory note is consistent with that source limitation. This audit independently consulted the primary text and other scholarly reference material, but those sources are not currently listed in the article or dataset.
claim_evidence.limitation: Dataset metadata and expansion-record checks do not demonstrate that a source passage supports a claim. The expansion record’s 31 October keyword count was not used as evidence.
claim_evidence.location: Matching record for ID euthyphro-dilemma; references array and date_verified field. Article §§9–10 for its further reading and attribution note.

issues.article_claim: ‘Divine command theorists accept the first horn but argue that God’s nature is essentially good, so commands are not arbitrary.’
issues.evidence_basis: SEP and IEP describe multiple versions and replies rather than a single position held by all divine-command theorists. SEP distinguishes Quinn, Adams, Hare, and Zagzebski; IEP sections 4.a–d separate accepting the cruelty implication, human-nature arguments, Alston’s account, and modified theory.
issues.recommended_action: Attribute the essential-nature reply to a specified version or named author, and avoid saying divine-command theorists as a group accept the first horn.

issues.article_claim: ‘Natural-law and rationalist views accept the second horn: reasons for action are available to human reason and God’s commands track them.’
issues.evidence_basis: SEP’s natural-law discussion identifies distinct positions and explicit disagreements, including Finnis’s practical-reason account and Jean Porter’s criticism; the consulted source does not establish that natural law and rationalist views uniformly accept this horn or that all hold the stated formulation.
issues.recommended_action: Present this as one possible family of responses, with named examples and a qualification that natural-law and rationalist accounts differ.

issues.article_claim: ‘Modified approaches locate goodness in God’s nature, so the choice is a false dichotomy.’
issues.evidence_basis: IEP discusses modified divine-command theory and Alston’s claim that God’s necessarily good character can be the supreme standard; SEP describes other strategies, including Adams’s distinction between good and right. The cited sources do not support treating these as one settled solution that simply makes the dilemma a false dichotomy.
issues.recommended_action: Name the relevant modified account and explain briefly how it responds to the dilemma; frame it as a proposed reply, not a resolved result.

issues.article_claim: ‘Secular critics use the argument to show that moral authority does not require a divine source.’
issues.evidence_basis: The consulted SEP and IEP passages document competing theistic accounts and non-theistic moral approaches, but do not establish that secular critics as a class use this argument for that conclusion. That conclusion is distinct from the dilemma’s challenge to a particular divine-command account.
issues.recommended_action: Either name a specific critic and source for this use, or recast as the article’s own possible implication rather than a general claim about secular critics.

issues.article_claim: ‘The major traditions have long-developed answers.’
issues.evidence_basis: SEP and IEP offer a selection of named historical and contemporary responses, but ‘major traditions’ is undefined and broader than the material consulted; the sources present disagreements rather than one answer or consensus.
issues.recommended_action: Replace the generalization with a short list of named replies and say that they remain disputed.

issues.article_claim: The entry attributes its account to the SEP reference but lists no direct edition or link to Plato’s Euthyphro; its attribution note says the primary text was not independently retrieved when drafted.
issues.evidence_basis: The matching dataset record lists only SEP Religion and Morality. This audit read the complete MIT-hosted Jowett translation’s relevant passages and confirmed that the question at 9e–11b follows Euthyphro’s definition of piety as what all the gods love.
issues.recommended_action: Add a direct primary-text citation in the article and dataset (with translator/edition clearly identified), while retaining SEP as secondary interpretation.

issues.article_claim: ‘Plato, Euthyphro (fourth century BCE)’ as a publication/date claim.
issues.evidence_basis: The page metadata for the MIT-hosted translation labels the dialogue ‘Written 380 B.C.E.’; the SEP shorter-works entry describes it as an early dialogue but does not establish a precise date. This supports the broad period only indirectly.
issues.recommended_action: Keep the broad ‘fourth century BCE’ approximation, identify it as an approximate conventional date, and avoid relying on the translation page’s hosting metadata as the sole dating authority.

article_edit_recommendations: Add a direct source for Plato’s Euthyphro, with translation/edition identified, to both the article’s Further Reading/Sources and the matching dataset references.
Revise §4 to distinguish particular divine-command and modified-theory replies, and avoid assigning natural-law, rationalist, or secular positions wholesale to either horn.
Name the authors or theories behind representative replies; state that their success and implications are disputed rather than implying a settled answer.
Retain the clear separation between Plato’s piety/all-gods question and later monotheistic moral-command formulations, and keep teaching analogies identified as the article’s own extensions.
Keep the date at the broad fourth-century BCE level and label it approximate.
entries.summary: I independently accessed the complete text page of Plato’s Euthyphro and read relevant passages alongside the relevant sections of the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (SEP) and Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy (IEP). The setup, the question at Euthyphro 10a, the basic dilemma, and its relevance to divine-command views are traceable. The dataset and article agree on ID, title, associated thinker, fourth-century BCE period, SEP reference, verification date, and related entries; the expansion record’s keyword count was not treated as evidence. The article’s classification of whole schools as accepting particular horns, its account of modified views, and its broad claim about secular critics and ‘major traditions’ need narrower, named attributions. The primary dialogue is not presently listed among the article’s or dataset’s references, although the article transparently says it was not consulted when written. Recommend adding a direct primary-text reference and revising the broad interpretive claims before treating the entry as fully source-checked. This is an editorial traceability review, not a judgment on the arguments’ soundness, an inference of consensus, or human expert review.
entries.confidence: High for the primary-text setup and question, the match between article and dataset metadata, and the identified overgeneralizations; moderate for broad chronology and the scope of the article’s claims about traditions, since the review was limited to the cited/reference sources and relevant passages rather than an exhaustive literature review.
first_pass_unresolved: The article gives no named source for the generalized claim about secular critics; evidence for that particular claim was not found in the consulted passages.
The consulted sources do not establish what counts as ‘the major traditions’ or justify a comprehensive claim that they all have long-developed answers; the article should name a bounded selection.

The full scholarly dispute about Plato’s composition date and the interpretation of the dialogue’s final aporia was not exhaustively researched. SEP’s Section 13 records more than one interpretation, and this review does not infer consensus.
No human subject-matter expert review was conducted.

entries.title: The Terror Bomber and the Tactical Bomber
entries.status_before: Not recorded in the supplied article or target dataset record; the expansion record reports only page/topic checks.
entries.scope: Claim-to-source traceability for setup, attribution, argument structure, conclusions, important qualifications, publication/name/date claims, and claims about scholarly disagreement. No files modified; no human expert review claimed.
entries.reviewer_type: AI-assisted claim-level source audit by a dedicated agent; no human expert review is claimed.

sources.access_level: Relevant passages read in the complete HTML entry; no printed page numbers, so section and paragraph/topic locations are given.
sources.author: Alison McIntyre
locations_read: Entry metadata and citation information: first-publication and revision dates; author listed at entry end.
Section 1, paragraphs on Aquinas, later formulations, four conditions, proportionality, and minimizing harm.
Section 2, ‘Terror bomber vs Tactical bomber’ paragraph; section 2 trolley-problem example.
Section 3, first and third misinterpretations, especially proportionality and minimizing harms.

Section 4.1, consequentialist objections; section 4.2, problem of closeness; section 4.3, side-effect effect; section 4.4, Quinn’s direct/indirect agency proposal; section 4.5, trolley-case disagreement; section 4.7, warfare norms and civilian precautions.
Section 6, critiques of whether one principle explains the cases and intentions’ relation to permissibility and deliberation.
Bibliography entries for Aquinas, Anscombe, Delaney, Lackey, Mangan, and other works cited in the entry.
sources.publication: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; first published 28 July 2004, substantive revision 17 July 2023
sources.role: The article’s sole reference and the target dataset record’s sole reference. It directly supports the central contrast and gives qualifications and a map of selected disagreements; it is not a primary source for the bomber example’s historical origin, and its bibliography alone does not establish the arguments of works listed there.
sources.title: Doctrine of Double Effect

claim_evidence.claim: The bomber contrast illustrates that harm intended as a means can be impermissible where the same harm is merely foreseen as a side effect; the article’s tactical bomber targets a munitions factory and the terror bomber targets civilian neighbourhoods to weaken morale and end the war sooner.
claim_evidence.finding: McIntyre’s section 2 gives the core contrast: the terror bomber aims to cause civilian deaths to weaken enemy resolve, while the tactical bomber aims at military targets and foresees civilian deaths; it says equal certainty of the same number of deaths does not erase the difference in the example. It does not specify a munitions factory, civilian neighbourhoods, or a goal of ending the war sooner.
claim_evidence.limitation: The factory, neighbourhood, just-war stipulation, and sooner-ending-war phrasing are article-authored scenario choices, not details verified from this cited passage. The source stipulates equal certainty of the same civilian death toll, not equal likelihood of shortening the war.
claim_evidence.location: Section 2, paragraph headed ‘Terror bomber vs Tactical bomber’.
claim_evidence.relationship: Supports the central contrast; does not establish the article’s added narrative details.

claim_evidence.claim: The two plans are otherwise outcome-equivalent: the article stipulates the same civilian death toll and that they are equally likely to shorten the war.
claim_evidence.finding: The SEP example stipulates equal certainty that the plans cause the same number of civilian deaths. It does not stipulate equal likelihood of shortening the war or otherwise describe their strategic outcomes as identical.
claim_evidence.limitation: This is a teaching-case stipulation, not a factual claim about military operations. It may alter the original example and should not be attributed to McIntyre without further evidence.
claim_evidence.location: Section 2, ‘Terror bomber vs Tactical bomber’ paragraph; compare the article’s section 1, paragraph 2.
claim_evidence.relationship: The death-toll stipulation is directly supported; the equal-likelihood claim is not established by the source and should be identified as the article’s own added assumption.

claim_evidence.claim: The doctrine of double effect says that foreseen side-effect harm may sometimes be permissible when the same harm would not be permissible as a means; proportionality and other conditions still matter.
claim_evidence.finding: The SEP introduction states the core distinction. Section 1 sets out formulations requiring, among other things, an otherwise permissible act, no intention of the bad effect, no production of the good effect by means of the bad, and a proportionately grave reason. It also discusses minimizing harm and alternatives. Section 3 explicitly warns that foreseeing harm is not by itself enough to establish permissibility.
claim_evidence.limitation: The doctrine has multiple formulations; ‘necessary’ is not presented as a single universal condition in the cited formulations. The article’s summary should not imply intention alone makes an attack permissible.
claim_evidence.location: Introduction; section 1, paragraphs on the New Catholic Encyclopedia conditions, Mangan’s formulation, and minimizing harm; section 3, first misinterpretation.

claim_evidence.claim: The bomber contrast reflects a widely shared judgment, and the tactical bomber may still be permissible only if proportionate and necessary; the terror bomber’s intentional targeting is treated as far worse.
claim_evidence.finding: Section 2 says the terror bombing is impermissible and tactical bombing permissible in the stipulated case. Section 4.7 says the judgment that terror bombing is impermissible and tactical bombing permissible is ‘widely affirmed,’ but then says the common judgment about tactical bombing deserves more scrutiny, discusses civilian-protection duties, and concludes that double effect—even with proportionality—does not supply a sufficient condition for permissible bombardment. The source does not characterize the contrast as ‘far worse’ or make ‘necessary’ the sole additional condition.
claim_evidence.limitation: This is McIntyre’s report and analysis, not evidence of universal agreement or legal permissibility. The article should avoid implying that proportionality and intention exhaust the conditions for lawful or ethical bombing.
claim_evidence.location: Section 2, ‘Terror bomber vs Tactical bomber’; section 4.7, paragraphs on the widely affirmed judgment and customary humanitarian-law precautions, especially the conclusion at the end of the section.
claim_evidence.relationship: Supports the illustrative contrast and the limited observation that the judgment is widely affirmed in the author’s account; qualifies a simple permissibility conclusion.

claim_evidence.claim: Defenders say intended harm treats a victim as an instrument, whereas side-effect harm does not; critics deny independent moral significance or object that intention descriptions can be manipulated; hybrid views say intention changes quality of will without changing permissibility, or the reverse.
claim_evidence.finding: The SEP supports some critics’ denial that intended/foreseen distinctions have moral significance, but stresses that many criticisms instead challenge application or explanatory adequacy. It discusses closeness and the side-effect effect, where normative judgments may bias descriptions. It presents Quinn’s direct/indirect agency proposal as one account, not as the view of all defenders. Section 6, with McCarthy and Scanlon, supports the direction that intention may matter to deliberation or moral assessment without changing permissibility. The cited passages do not establish the article’s ‘or the reverse’ hybrid category.
claim_evidence.limitation: The SEP’s surveyed disagreement is not an exhaustive taxonomy or consensus claim. ‘Victim as an instrument’ should be attributed to a specific account if retained; the reverse hybrid position needs its own cited source or should be removed.
claim_evidence.location: Sections 4.1–4.4 and 6, especially 4.1 (paragraphs distinguishing consequentialist and other criticism), 4.3 (side-effect effect), 4.4 (Quinn), and section 6 (McCarthy/Scanlon discussion).
claim_evidence.relationship: Partially supports; the article compresses distinct views and includes an untraced position.

claim_evidence.claim: The case matters for law and ethics in conflict, medicine, and policing, where an agent’s aim is said to change the nature of an act.
claim_evidence.finding: The SEP discusses wartime civilian harm and international humanitarian-law precautions, and separately discusses end-of-life medicine. The consulted passages do not establish a policing application or a general claim that law across these domains uses the same intention-based test.
claim_evidence.limitation: The source is a philosophical reference entry, not a jurisdiction-specific legal authority. Policing and legal claims require separate, directly relevant sources or should be explicitly framed as prospective applications.
claim_evidence.location: Section 4.7, discussion of warfare norms and ICRC rules; section 5, end-of-life decision-making; compare the article’s section 3, paragraph 2.
claim_evidence.relationship: Contextual support for war and medical-ethics relevance; does not establish the policing or broad legal generalization.

claim_evidence.claim: The doctrine’s roots are medieval, the bomber pair arose in twentieth-century discussion, and no single originator is identified.
claim_evidence.finding: Section 1 credits Thomas Aquinas with introducing the doctrine in discussion of self-defense and identifies later formulations. The entry’s bomber paragraph does not identify an originator or date for that example. Its bibliography includes twentieth-century scholarship, including Delaney’s 2008 ‘Two Cheers for “Closeness”: Terror, Targeting and Double Effect,’ but that listing does not establish when or by whom the example was first introduced.
claim_evidence.limitation: The article’s wording ‘sources consulted’ is appropriately limited if it means this SEP entry, but neither it nor the dataset’s reference supports a historical date for the bomber scenario. Do not infer that no originator exists.
claim_evidence.location: Section 1, opening historical paragraphs; section 2, bomber paragraph; bibliography entries for Delaney (2008), Anscombe (1982), and others.
claim_evidence.relationship: Supports medieval doctrinal roots; does not establish the bomber pair’s publication history or first attribution.

claim_evidence.claim: The article’s trolley comparison, applications and variations are source-derived extensions of the bomber case.
claim_evidence.finding: The SEP separately discusses trolley cases and the means/side-effect distinction, which supports the article’s broad comparison. It does not establish the article’s own discussion prompts or all of its proposed variations about civilian numbers and success likelihood.
claim_evidence.limitation: Teaching questions are not historical or scholarly claims. Keep them labeled as prompts, and present effects of changing numbers or likelihood as an analysis of the hypothetical rather than a reported source claim.
claim_evidence.location: Section 2, trolley-problem application; sections 4.5 and 6, trolley disagreement and examples.
claim_evidence.relationship: Supports the general contextual comparison; the prompts and proposed variations are editorial framing/inference.

issues.article_claim: The article’s original-publication metadata says the bomber example was developed in twentieth-century discussion; its attribution paragraph says no single originator was named in the sources consulted.
issues.evidence_basis: The consulted SEP text credits Aquinas for the doctrine’s introduction and discusses the bomber pair without assigning its origin or date. The bibliography’s later works do not establish first publication. The dataset has the same metadata and only the SEP reference; the expansion record expressly reports page/topic checks, not passage verification.
issues.recommended_action: Separate the doctrine’s medieval roots from the bomber example’s unverified publication history. Retain the limited ‘not attributed in the consulted entry’ wording, and state that the example’s origin/date has not been established unless a source documenting it is added.

issues.article_claim: The pilots have equal likelihood of shortening the war; one attacks a munitions factory and the other civilian neighbourhoods to end the war sooner.
issues.evidence_basis: SEP section 2 describes military targets, enemy resolve, and equal certainty of the same civilian death toll, but not these added details or equal likelihood of success.
issues.recommended_action: Either align the scenario with the SEP’s description or explicitly label these as author-added stipulations; avoid implying the equal-likelihood assumption is part of the cited source.

issues.article_claim: Tactical bombing is presented as acceptable if proportionate and necessary, and the contrast is said to match a widely shared judgment about war.
issues.evidence_basis: SEP section 4.7 reports the judgment as widely affirmed, but emphasizes that proportionality alone does not establish permissibility and discusses precautions, warnings, and civilian-protection rules; section 1 also supports minimizing harm and considering less harmful alternatives.

claim_evidence.claim: Smith stands to inherit if his six-year-old cousin dies, drowns him in the bath, and arranges the scene to look accidental; Jones shares the motive and intended outcome, but sees the child fall into the water and watches, prepared to push his head under if necessary.
claim_evidence.finding: The primary text gives these material details, including the child’s age, inheritance motive, Jones’s plan, the accidental fall, and his readiness to push the child’s head back under. The entry is a fair paraphrase of the setup.
claim_evidence.limitation: The precise article wording is more informative than a compressed retelling: Jones sees the child slip and hit his head, and is delighted; the setup is not an ordinary rescue case.
claim_evidence.location: Printed p. 79, Smith/Jones case paragraphs (reprint PDF p. 3); moral comparison continues on reprint PDF p. 4.

claim_evidence.claim: ‘The motives, knowledge and results are the same.’
claim_evidence.finding: Rachels explicitly says the men have the same motive and ‘exactly the same end in view’; both children die. But the broad assertion that their knowledge is the same is not established: the described events differ, and Jones sees the child’s accidental fall while Smith deliberately drowns him. The claim needs to specify which knowledge is meant rather than imply every relevant circumstance is identical.
claim_evidence.limitation: This flags an ambiguity/overstatement, not a claim that Rachels’s intended comparison is invalid. SEP describes the cases as designed to hold factors constant but notes that this equality is challenged.
claim_evidence.location: Printed p. 79, case description and paragraph beginning ‘Now Smith killed the child…’ (reprint PDF pp. 3–4). Compare SEP §1, first paragraph on the contrast strategy.

claim_evidence.claim: Smith acts while Jones ‘merely allows’ the death; Rachels uses their apparent moral equivalence to challenge the intrinsic moral significance of killing versus letting die.
claim_evidence.finding: Rachels explicitly says Jones’s defense that he only let the child die is no defense, and argues that the bare difference between killing and letting die makes no moral difference in itself. SEP §1 accurately characterizes the inference from case-level equivalence to the claim about killing and letting die per se.
claim_evidence.limitation: The case-level judgment and the general inference are distinct. SEP documents challenges to both the equalization of the cases and the inference from the pair to general moral equivalence.
claim_evidence.location: §1, opening paragraphs on Rachels’s contrast strategy and the two claims the argument depends on; corroborated by Rachels, printed p. 79.

claim_evidence.claim: Many people and many professional codes assume that causing death is worse than failing to prevent it.
claim_evidence.finding: The primary article reports Rachels’s claim that the doctrine seems accepted by most doctors and reproduces one AMA policy statement. The sources consulted do not establish the broader plural claim about ‘many professional codes.’
claim_evidence.limitation: No independent survey or review of multiple professional codes was consulted. The article’s wording generalizes beyond the specific evidence read.
claim_evidence.location: Printed p. 78, opening paragraphs and quoted AMA policy; printed p. 79, paragraph distinguishing typical cases from the bare distinction.

claim_evidence.claim: Rachels used the pair in an argument about the active/passive euthanasia distinction, including withdrawal of treatment versus directly ending a life.
claim_evidence.finding: The essay’s stated subject is active and passive euthanasia; the case appears in its discussion of whether killing is intrinsically worse than letting die, and Rachels explicitly applies that point to humane treatment decisions. The entry’s example is accurate when limited to the argument Rachels makes, not a claim that the analogy settles clinical or policy questions.
claim_evidence.limitation: Rachels’s essay challenges a moral distinction; it does not by itself settle the permissibility of any particular medical practice or policy.
claim_evidence.location: Printed p. 79, paragraphs following the Smith/Jones comparison and the paragraph beginning ‘Now, it may be pointed out…’; conclusion on printed p. 80.

claim_evidence.claim: The line between what we do and what we merely permit becomes harder to defend as a limit on our responsibilities if letting die is not intrinsically better than killing.
claim_evidence.finding: This is a further implication drawn by the entry, not a conclusion established in Rachels’s Smith/Jones argument. The SEP separately discusses the relevance of the distinction to responsibilities and aid, but the conditional move requires further premises.
claim_evidence.limitation: The entry should identify this as its own conditional implication, not attribute it to Rachels or present it as established by the case.
claim_evidence.location: Introduction on the relation of doing/allowing to aid and consequences; compare §1 on Rachels’s actual inference.

claim_evidence.claim: Rachels’s argument is that Smith and Jones are equally blameworthy, so act/omission has no intrinsic significance; the case does not establish that killing and letting die are always morally equal.
claim_evidence.finding: This is a broadly fair summary if ‘equally blameworthy’ is understood as a paraphrase of Rachels’s claim that neither behaved better and Jones’s letting-die defense has no moral weight. The final qualification is important and well-founded: Rachels explicitly allows that consequences may create important moral differences in some cases. SEP records challenges to the general inference.
claim_evidence.limitation: The source establishes what Rachels argued, not that the conclusion is true. ‘Act/omission’ should not be used as if identical to the doing/allowing distinction; SEP §2 warns against conflating them.
claim_evidence.location: Printed p. 79, moral assessment and application paragraphs; printed p. 80, final paragraph beginning ‘However, the preceding considerations…’. SEP §1 and §11 on limits and challenges to the inference.

claim_evidence.claim: Critics reply that the pair is stacked because both agents intend death, and that the contrast should be tested in ordinary rescue cases without murderous aims.
claim_evidence.finding: Intention and motive are discussed as possible limits on the inference: Brassington argues that differences in intent/motive matter in further cases, and Stempsey presents the shared wrongful intention as one possible response. However, the SEP presents several distinct objections: Hill challenges whether the pair is properly equalized; Kamm challenges the apparent moral equivalence; Kagan challenges the general inference. The ‘ordinary rescue’ formulation is better treated as the article’s teaching proposal than as a claim established about critics generally.
claim_evidence.limitation: Do not imply that all critics advance an intention objection or that it is the principal scholarly response. The sources document disagreement, not a consensus.
claim_evidence.location: §1, paragraphs on Hill, Kamm, and Kagan; §11, paragraphs summarizing distinct objections. Compare Brassington, ‘Rachels on killing and letting die,’ and Stempsey, ‘Causation and Moral Responsibility for Death,’ opening discussion.

entries.summary: The complete Rachels article was read in a university-hosted permissioned reprint, and its title, author, date, volume, issue, and pages were confirmed against NEJM’s publisher record. The SEP’s Fall 2025 entry and relevant passages of Iain Brassington’s full scholarly article were also read. They support the scenario and Rachels’s central argument, while documenting substantive, named objections and distinct defenses; they do not establish a consensus. The article generally tracks the primary source, but “same ... knowledge” overstates the case’s sameness, “many professional codes” is not established by the sources consulted, and the disagreement summary blends a documented concern about intention with an uncited teaching recommendation and does not name the distinct objections. The dataset lists only the SEP reference; its 2026-10-31 verification date reflects the page/topic-check process in expansion.md, not full passage review. claim_evidence.claim: Jim is offered the choice to kill one captive and release the other nineteen; refusing results in the captain’s execution of all twenty, and Williams presents utilitarianism as recommending that Jim shoot.
claim_evidence.finding: Williams’s original §3 directly presents the conditional offer, the threatened execution of all twenty on refusal, and says that utilitarianism replies that Jim should kill one. He qualifies the verdict with “if the situations are essentially as described and there are no further special factors.”
claim_evidence.limitation: Williams states the utilitarian verdict under the hypothetical’s terms; this does not establish that every consequentialist variant endorses it or that the utilitarian answer is the final moral answer.
claim_evidence.location: Williams, “A Critique of Utilitarianism,” §3, “Negative responsibility: and two examples,” Jim passage and paragraph beginning “To these dilemmas”; print pp. 97–99 (page references cross-confirmed in the SEP Williams entry and Venkatesh §2).

claim_evidence.claim: The article stipulates that Jim cannot stop the executions by force, that the captain will keep his word, and that no one else can intervene.
claim_evidence.finding: Williams says Jim’s own attempt to overpower the captain and soldiers would fail and lead to all being killed, including Jim, and says the captain will release the others if Jim accepts. The source does not explicitly rule out every possible third-party intervention, nor independently establish the captain’s reliability as a real-world matter. The article presents these as assumptions, making them editorial constraints rather than direct historical/source claims.
claim_evidence.limitation: The ‘no one else can intervene’ and ‘captain will keep his word’ formulations are not exact statements in Williams’s text. They are permissible scenario stipulations only if clearly identified as the article’s simplifications.
claim_evidence.location: Williams, “A Critique of Utilitarianism,” §3, Jim passage, print pp. 97–99.

claim_evidence.claim: The article describes its retelling as removing the original nationality and setting.
claim_evidence.finding: Williams locates Jim in a South American town and describes the captives as Indians; the article removes those particular geographic and identity labels. It retains a generic small-town setting, captain, armed forces, and execution scenario, so ‘setting removed’ overstates the change unless it means the specific setting.
claim_evidence.limitation: ‘Specific South American and Indigenous setting removed; generic town setting retained’ would be more precise.
claim_evidence.location: Williams, “A Critique of Utilitarianism,” §3, Jim passage, print pp. 97–99; compared with article §10, Sources and Attribution.

claim_evidence.claim: The article says the case targets a feature of act utilitarianism: the agent’s action is treated as one causal route among others toward an overall outcome, and it connects this to projects, commitments, and alienation.
claim_evidence.finding: Williams’s section on negative responsibility argues that consequentialism levels causal connections through one’s own and another’s agency; in the Jim discussion he connects this to responsibility and integrity. In §5 he argues that requiring an agent to set aside projects and convictions for the utility calculation alienates the agent from the action. The SEP Williams entry presents the objection as being about the first-personal character of agency, rather than merely an intuition that Jim must refuse.
claim_evidence.limitation: The article’s phrase ‘a particular feature of act utilitarianism’ appropriately narrows the immediate target; Williams’s discussion also treats wider forms of consequentialism and the issue is disputed.
claim_evidence.location: Williams §§3 and 5, especially the Jim discussion and integrity/project passages; compare SEP Bernard Williams §4, paragraphs on negative responsibility and the integrity objection.

claim_evidence.claim: Williams’s point is not that Jim must refuse or that integrity always overrides saving lives; he does not claim Jim is certainly wrong to shoot.
claim_evidence.finding: Williams says the cases are not simple counterexamples based on utilitarianism choosing the wrong act; he allows that utilitarianism may be right in Jim’s case and says the problem concerns the considerations and agency involved in reaching the answer. The article’s qualification tracks the primary text and the SEP and Venkatesh interpretations.
claim_evidence.limitation: This is Williams’s stated qualification, not a conclusion that his argument succeeds or that all interpreters agree on its exact force.
claim_evidence.location: Williams §3, Jim discussion, print pp. 97–99; §5, integrity discussion (the SEP Williams entry cites Williams at UFA pp. 116–17 for the relevant qualification). Also Venkatesh, §2.

claim_evidence.claim: The article says Williams pairs Jim with a chemist who has qualms about weapons work.
claim_evidence.finding: Williams presents George’s chemical/biological warfare laboratory case immediately before Jim’s and uses both to introduce the discussion. This is a source-reported pairing, not a later teaching variation invented by the article.
claim_evidence.limitation: The article’s short description omits George’s family circumstances, alternative candidate, and other details; that is compression, not a contradiction.
claim_evidence.location: Williams §3, “Negative responsibility: and two examples,” George and Jim cases, print pp. 97–99.

claim_evidence.claim: The article’s ‘Major Interpretations’ paragraph says standard consequentialists endorse shooting and treat reluctance as understandable but not decisive; sophisticated consequentialists defend commitments because they have good effects; Williams doubts the theory can understand Jim’s agonizing choice; deontological and agent-relative views permit constraints or prerogatives.
claim_evidence.finding: The direct act-utilitarian recommendation and Williams qualification are supported. The SEP consequentialism entry distinguishes direct, indirect, virtue, and agent-relative approaches and describes alternative strategies, while Moseley treats Williams’s integrity critique as directed at act utilitarianism rather than all consequentialism. Venkatesh documents multiple interpretations and argues for one contested reading. These sources support a qualified map of debate, but not the article’s unnamed categories as a settled or exhaustive account; the claim about reluctance being ‘understandable but not decisive’ is an interpretive gloss rather than a clearly attributed source conclusion.
claim_evidence.limitation: The article’s broad labels are not sourced to specific authors or formulations, and the sources disagree about the objection’s scope and best interpretation.
